name: Bilal Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a mix of lectures and chaos. I'm training to be a primary school teacher, so I'm in lectures on how kids learn to read, and one day a week I'm shadowing in a Year 3 classroom, which I love. Three nights a week I work the concessions counter at the cinema on Mill Street, popcorn and drinks, until midnight. I share a flat with two other students above a kebab shop, and the heating is a rumour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you want from this degree when you chose it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly I'm okay at the degree and nervous about the money. My loan covers fees and nothing else, so the cinema pays my rent share. I've got about three weeks of expenses saved, if I'm careful. My parents live far away and can't send anything, so there's no safety net if the cinema cuts my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, mostly hype with a few useful bits. I'd tell my flatmates the tools are fine for summarising a reading, but they can't teach a seven-year-old to read. I'd probably say it online too, but less loudly than the people who say it's everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved and still worried. Relieved that teaching stays teaching. Worried because schools are already underfunded and class sizes are going up, and AI hype doesn't fix that. I keep seeing newly qualified teachers who can't find permanent posts near here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Finish the term, keep the Year 3 placement, and try to move my cinema shifts to weekends so they don't clash with essays. I'd use the AI tool now and again for turning a long article into notes, then check it. I'd also look for a paid tutoring gig, because it pays double the cinema.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit like a slow week. There's the usual background hum of money, but nothing new to panic about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI tools at the moment, if you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, maybe once a week. Last month I asked it to make a quiz on fractions, and half the questions were wrong, so I rewrote them. It saves me twenty minutes if I check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which is more likely to cause you trouble, the cinema hours or the cost of the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, definitely. Rent went up eight percent in September, and the landlord won't fix the shower. The cinema hours I can juggle. A bigger rent bill I can't. If it goes up again I'd have to move into a halls room across town or beg a friend's couch.

say: I'd tell flatmates AI is **good for summaries** but can't teach a seven-year-old to read.
I'd say the real problem for teachers is **funding**, not technology.
think: I'm relieved teaching stays teaching but worried about **class sizes** and few permanent posts nearby.
The **rent** worries me more than any technology: another rise would force me out of the flat.
do: Keep the Year 3 placement and move **cinema shifts** to weekends.
Use AI **once a week** for summaries, then check every line.
Look for paid **tutoring**, which pays about double the cinema.
feel: **Fine** mostly, with the usual background money hum.
S0.quote: I use it now and then, maybe once a week. Last month I asked it to make a quiz on fractions, and half the questions were wrong
fieldNote: Bilal is **steady** about AI: uses it weekly, checks it, and has a real example of it getting things wrong.
His main risk is **rent**, not technology; flat costs rose eight percent.
Calm about his degree, but the job market for new teachers nearby keeps him uneasy.

steps.text: Keep the Year 3 placement going all term
Find a paid tutoring gig on weekends
Use AI weekly for summaries and check every line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so teachers should have a say in how it's used. I'd back a union push for training time and for rules on children's data. Online I'd say AI can plan a lesson, but it can't notice the child at the back who's gone quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it will change teaching more than people admit. Marking, planning, reports to parents, all that gets automated, and a school might decide it needs fewer assistants. I'd be fine if my workload dropped, but I'd worry that schools use it as an excuse to cut staff to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly now, early, so I'm the new teacher who can show a school how to use them safely. I'd join the student branch of the teaching union and ask about their AI guidance. At the cinema they're already testing a self-service kiosk, so I'd ask for a few more daytime tutoring hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Interested and a bit protective. I like trying new tools, but I don't trust companies selling them to schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI do in a primary classroom that worries or interests you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Report writing, honestly. Teachers lose whole weekends writing the same sentence in thirty ways. If a tool drafts those and I edit, I'd get my Sunday back. What I'd worry about is software marking children's writing, because kids need a human saying well done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If schools hired fewer teachers, what's your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the schools in towns that struggle to recruit, where there's always a job, and I'd think about teaching assistant roles as a stepping stone. I wouldn't leave teaching. I'd keep a second string, like tutoring, so I'm not stuck relying on one contract.

say: I'd back a union push for **training time** and rules on children's data.
I'd say AI can plan a lesson but can't notice the **quiet child** at the back.
think: Marking, planning and reports will be automated, and schools may **cut assistants** to save money.
I'd happily lose the **Sunday report writing**, but I don't trust companies selling to schools.
do: Learn the tools **properly now** so I can show a school how to use them safely.
Join the student branch of the **teaching union** and ask about AI guidance.
Apply to schools in towns that struggle to **recruit** teachers.
feel: **Interested** and protective, with some distrust of the companies.
S1.quote: Teachers lose whole weekends writing the same sentence in thirty ways. If a tool drafts those and I edit, I'd get my Sunday back.
fieldNote: Bilal moves **early** on the tools and sees real upside in report writing.
His **union** instinct fits his progressive outlook: training time, data rules, staffing guarantees.
Anxious because assistants and cinema hours could go first, and he has only three weeks of savings.

steps.text: Learn AI report-drafting tools before the next placement
Join the teaching union's student branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, schools least of all. I'd say governments have to slow down how it's rolled out, or at least pay for people to cope. Two years is one school year and a bit. We can't retrain a whole country's teachers in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be shaken. I'd be in my third year when it lands, and there might be no need for a whole classroom of adults. Maybe parents still want a human, but the money for staff might vanish. I don't know, and that's the awful bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the degree, because a teaching qualification is still a ticket to a classroom. I'd push my union to ask for guarantees on staff numbers. I'd keep working at the cinema as long as it lasts, save every spare pound, and talk to my tutors about what schools are planning. I'd also keep trying tools, because avoiding them wouldn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not frozen. It's like waiting for exam results, a bit sick but you get on with the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually tell your parents about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone my mum and say it plainly: I'm staying in the degree, but I might need to come home if rent and the loan get tough. She'd say come home, whatever happens. That's the plan B I'm lucky to have, even if she can't send money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots matter for a teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot. A child needs a person physically in the room, and robots that can handle a classroom are years off. So teaching might hold longer than office work. I'd still be nervous, because the planning and marking go on the stated date and schools might shrink first.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and governments must slow the roll-out or pay for people to cope.
I'd tell my mum I'm staying on the degree but may **come home**.
think: I'm **shaken**: schools might still want humans but the money for staff could vanish.
Teaching may hold longer than office work, because robots in a **classroom** are years off.
do: Stay on the degree and press the union for **staff number guarantees**.
Keep the cinema job and save **every spare pound**.
Ask tutors what **local schools** plan for the next two years.
feel: **Scared** but not frozen, like waiting for exam results.
S2.quote: A child needs a person physically in the room, and robots that can handle a classroom are years off.
fieldNote: Bilal separates **thinking AI** now from classroom robots later, and uses the 3-year gap to stay hopeful.
His **plan B** is moving home, which softens the fear.
He keeps a union demand rather than a personal exit plan, true to his progressive outlook.

steps.text: Stay on the teaching degree and keep placements
Ask the union for guarantees on school staff numbers
Save every spare pound from the cinema job
Agree with my mum that I can move home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning and we should treat it as one. Five years is enough to train properly if the money is there. I'd say employers and schools should publish what they're planning so students know what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years works for me. I'd qualify in three, then have two years in a classroom before the thinking AI is fully there. If robots in classrooms are a decade away, a good teacher might still have a job through most of my twenties. I'm hopeful but I'd keep a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, apply early to schools, and spend my first teaching year learning the AI tools properly. I'd get a second qualification, maybe special educational needs, because it's something human and harder to replace. And I'd carry on with a bit of tutoring on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously okay. It gives me room to breathe, and I like having a window to make decisions rather than a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be half-trained and shocked. With five, I'd be a qualified teacher with some savings and time to specialise. The difference is whether I'm choosing or just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start a special educational needs certificate in my first year, since that work needs patience and a person in the room, and join the union branch as a rep. Then I'd save a tenth of my pay. That's the plan.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** and schools should publish their plans so students know what to study.
I'd tell friends to specialise in work that needs a **person in the room**.
think: Five years works: I'd qualify in three and get **two classroom years** before the thinking AI is everywhere.
I stay hopeful but keep a **plan B**, because school budgets are unpredictable.
do: Finish the degree and apply **early** to schools.
Spend my first teaching year learning AI tools **properly**.
Start a **special educational needs** certificate alongside the job.
feel: **Cautiously okay**, glad to be choosing rather than reacting.
S3.quote: With two years, I'd be half-trained and shocked. With five, I'd be a qualified teacher with some savings and time to specialise.
fieldNote: Bilal sees time as the difference between **choosing and reacting**.
His plan builds a **human-only niche**: special educational needs and union work.
Uneasy, not calm, because school funding stays uncertain.

steps.text: Start a special educational needs certificate in my first teaching year
Learn AI planning tools properly in my first year teaching
Save a tenth of every teaching pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time to do it right. Ten years is a whole teaching career's first stage. I'd say governments should be rewriting the curriculum now, with more on talking, arguing, making things and looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough. I'd be a few years into a teaching job by 2036, probably with my own class and maybe a deputy role by then. Teaching would change, but I'd be inside the change rather than watching it. I might worry for older teachers more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard, finish, teach in a school that trains its staff, and build up a master's part-time later. I'd save into a pension from day one. And I'd be that person at school who learns each new tool first and shares it with the team, because that makes me useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful. It feels like a big change I can ride, and that's rare for me, since I normally feel one step from broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever technology comes, I'd want schools to protect play, reading aloud and a real teacher knowing every child's name. Those are the bits that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd want schools to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to take a deputy or subject lead role by my early thirties and think about teacher training. That's the part that machines can't do, helping new teachers feel less alone.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to do it right, and the curriculum should teach talking, making and caring.
I'd tell colleagues to protect **play and reading aloud**.
think: Ten years feels like enough: I'd be **inside the change** rather than watching it from outside.
I'd worry more about **older teachers** than about myself.
do: Finish the degree and join a school that **trains its staff**.
Build a **master's** part-time once I'm settled.
Pay into a **pension** from the first pay slip.
feel: Pretty **hopeful**, which is rare for someone usually one step from broke.
S4.quote: Whatever technology comes, I'd want schools to protect play, reading aloud and a real teacher knowing every child's name.
fieldNote: Bilal is **hopeful** because ten years gives him a teaching career inside the change.
He frames his future around **schools and colleagues**, not just himself.
The calm reflects a stable qualification and long time horizon, though the present rent still bites.

steps.text: Study a part-time master's in education once settled
Learn each new classroom tool first and share it with colleagues
Pay into a pension from the first pay slip

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be in the middle of my degree with rent due and nothing set. What would help is clear honesty from the university and government, protected funding for teaching jobs, and rent help for students. Even a rent cap would do more than any speech about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that students like me aren't against technology. We want a say in how it comes into classrooms. Ask us before you decide for us.

headlineQuote: Students like me aren't against technology. We want a say in how it comes into classrooms.
portrait: Bilal is a **19-year-old** first-year primary teaching student who shares a cold flat and works nights at a cinema.
He is progressive and **union-minded**, wanting a say in how technology reaches schools.
He uses AI **once a week** for summaries and checks the answers, a steady and pragmatic habit.
His mood ranges from calm at ten years to **anxious** when assistant jobs and rent are at risk.
He sees teaching as a **human job** that holds longer than office work, and plans a special needs niche.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because he would be mid-degree with rent due and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Honest early word from **university and government**, protected teaching funding and student rent help.
